title: FLEX vs. SMILE: A Deep Dive into Lenticule Extraction Refractive Surgery
summary: Explore Femtosecond Lenticule Extraction (FLEX) and Small Incision Lenticule Extraction (SMILE), two advanced femtosecond laser-based refractive procedures. This comprehensive guide dissects their mechanisms, patient selection, surgical techniques, and outcomes, highlighting key differences and clinical implications for ophthalmology residents and fellows.

sections.title: 1. Definition & Overview
sections.content: Femtosecond Lenticule Extraction (FLEX) and Small Incision Lenticule Extraction (SMILE) are keratorefractive procedures utilizing a femtosecond laser to create an intrastromal lenticule, which is then removed to correct refractive errors. FLEX, a precursor to SMILE, involved creating a corneal flap similar to LASIK. SMILE refined this by eliminating the need for a full flap, instead creating a small incision for lenticule extraction, aiming for enhanced corneal biomechanical stability and reduced dry eye symptoms.

sections.title: 2. Epidemiology & Demographics
content: **Prevalence:** Myopia affects 30-40% of adults in developed countries, driving demand for refractive surgery.
**SMILE Growth:** Rapidly gaining popularity globally, especially in Asia, due to flapless nature.
**Ideal Candidates:** Typically adults 18-45 years old with stable myopia (-0.5 to -10.0 D) or myopic astigmatism (up to -5.0 D).
**Global Reach:** Over 10 million SMILE procedures performed worldwide since its introduction.

sections.title: Risk Factors / Contraindications
content: Unstable Refraction: Change >0.5 D/year.
Keratoconus/Pellucid Marginal Degeneration (PMD): Any corneal ectasia.
Thin Cornea: Residual stromal bed <250 µm after ablation.
Severe Dry Eye Syndrome: Pre-existing ocular surface disease.
Collagen Vascular Disease: Rheumatoid arthritis, SLE (impaired healing).
Immunosuppression: Increased risk of infection/poor healing.
Pregnancy/Lactation: Hormonal fluctuations affect corneal hydration and refraction.
Glaucoma/Ocular Hypertension: IOP spikes during suction.
Severe Blepharitis/Meibomian Gland Dysfunction: Increased infection risk.
Monocular Patients: Relative contraindication.

sections.title: 3. Etiology & Pathophysiology
sections.content: Both FLEX and SMILE correct refractive error by precisely removing an intrastromal lenticule of corneal tissue. The femtosecond laser (e.g., Carl Zeiss VisuMax) creates micro-cavitation bubbles through photodisruption, separating corneal tissue layers. The shape and thickness of the lenticule are customized based on the patient's refractive error, determined by pre-operative topography and wavefront analysis. Removing this lenticule alters the anterior corneal curvature, thus changing its refractive power. SMILE's key advantage lies in preserving the anterior corneal lamellae and Bowman's layer integrity outside the small incision, leading to superior biomechanical stability compared to flap-based procedures like LASIK and FLEX. This preservation minimizes nerve severance, potentially reducing post-operative dry eye.

branches: **FLEX (Femtosecond Lenticule Extraction)**: Flap-based removal of intrastromal lenticule.
**SMILE (Small Incision Lenticule Extraction)**: Flapless, cap-based removal via small incision.
**ReLEX (Refractive Lenticule Extraction)**: Term encompasses both FLEX and SMILE, though often used synonymously with SMILE due to its prevalence.
**Contoura Vision SMILE (Next-gen)**: Combines topography-guided ablation with SMILE for enhanced precision.

sections.title: 5. Clinical Features & Symptoms (Post-Op)
content: **Visual Recovery**: Good functional vision by day 1, stabilizes over weeks.
**Mild Discomfort**: Foreign body sensation, tearing, photophobia (12-24 hrs post-SMILE, similar to LASIK post-FLEX).
**Halo/Glare**: Transient, especially at night, improving over months.
**Dry Eye Symptoms**: Less severe and shorter duration with SMILE vs. FLEX/LASIK.
**Fluctuating Vision**: Common in early post-op period due to corneal hydration/healing.
**Subconjunctival Hemorrhage**: Due to suction, resolves in 1-2 weeks.

sections.title: 6. Investigations & Diagnostic Workup
content: **Step 1: Comprehensive Ophthalmic History & Examination** - Refractive stability, systemic health, ocular history, current medications.
**Step 2: Manifest & Cycloplegic Refraction** - Accurate measure of refractive error, particularly for hyperopes and young patients.
**Step 3: Best Corrected Visual Acuity (BCVA) Assessment** - Rule out underlying ocular pathology.
**Step 4: Slit-lamp Biomicroscopy** - Anterior segment health, tear film evaluation (Schirmer test, TBUT, OSDI questionnaire).
**Step 5: Intraocular Pressure (IOP) Measurement** - Baseline check for glaucoma.
**Step 6: Dilated Fundus Examination** - Rule out peripheral retinal pathology (e.g., tears, lattice degeneration).

**Step 7: Corneal Topography & Tomography (e.g., Pentacam HR, Orbscan IIz, Sirius)** - Essential for ruling out ectatic disorders (keratoconus, PMD), assessing CCT, anterior/posterior corneal elevation, pachymetry progression maps, epithelial maps (for subtle ectasia).
**Step 8: Optical Coherence Tomography (OCT)** - Anterior segment OCT (AS-OCT) for detailed corneal layer assessment, epithelial thickness mapping, residual stromal bed estimation.
**Step 9: Wavefront Aberrometry** - Measures higher-order aberrations (HOAs) to predict potential night vision issues (less critical for SMILE/FLEX vs. wavefront-guided LASIK).
**Step 10: Specular Microscopy (Endothelial Cell Count)** - Important for patients with previous ocular surgery or suspected endothelial compromise.

sections.title: 9. Management & Treatment (Post-operative)
content: **Immediate Post-op (Day 0-7):**
**Topical Steroids:** e.g., Prednisolone Acetate 1% QID for 1-2 weeks (e.g., FML 0.1% for 3-4 weeks for SMILE) to reduce inflammation and prevent haze.
**Topical Antibiotics:** e.g., Moxifloxacin 0.5% QID for 1 week to prevent infection.
**Artificial Tears (Preservative-free):** QID to hourly as needed for dry eye relief.
**NSAID Drops:** (Optional) for pain relief, e.g., Ketorolac 0.4% BID-TID for a few days.
**Protective Eyewear:** Eye shields at night, sunglasses outdoors for 1 week.
**Subsequent Weeks/Months:**
**Steroid Taper:** Gradually taper steroids based on inflammation.
**Continued Lubrication:** As needed, may continue for several months post-SMILE.
**Refractive Enhancement:** If significant residual refractive error after 3-6 months, consider PRK (most common for SMILE/FLEX) or relift (FLEX/LASIK).
**Management of Complications:**
**DLK:** Aggressive topical steroids (e.g., Prednisolone Acetate 1% q1h), consider oral steroids. Interface irrigation for Grade 3/4.
**Infection:** Immediate culture, broad-spectrum fortified antibiotics (e.g., Vancomycin + Ceftazidime), potentially corneal scrape/biopsy.
**Epithelial Ingrowth:** Observation for Grade 1. Surgical debridement with flap lift, scraping, polishing, +/- fibrin glue, +/- alcohol for Grade 2/3 (FLEX/LASIK).
**Corneal Ectasia:** Cross-linking (CXL) to stabilize the cornea.

sections.title: 12. Red Flags / Emergency Signs (Post-Op)
content: Sudden, severe decrease in vision.
Intense or worsening eye pain not relieved by OTC analgesics.
Redness of the eye that rapidly worsens or is accompanied by discharge.
New onset or worsening photophobia (light sensitivity).
Progressive white or opaque area on the cornea.
Swelling of the eyelids.
Any signs of flap dislocation (in FLEX/LASIK) - significant blurring, foreign body sensation, wrinkling visible.

content.explanation: Helps remember SMILE's key benefits: superior biomechanical stability due to flapless nature (stronger mechanics) and its core principle (lenticule extraction).

sections.title: 14. Key Clinical Pearls
content: **SMILE's Biomechanical Advantage:** Preserves more anterior stromal lamellae and Bowman's layer integrity compared to LASIK/FLEX, leading to better corneal biomechanical strength.
**Dry Eye Mitigation:** SMILE severs fewer corneal nerves, resulting in a significantly lower incidence and severity of post-operative dry eye symptoms compared to LASIK/FLEX.
**Learning Curve:** SMILE has a steeper learning curve for surgeons, particularly in lenticule dissection and extraction.

**Visual Recovery:** While SMILE patients often report feeling better sooner, initial visual acuity may be slightly slower to achieve optimal levels compared to LASIK/FLEX in some studies, but rapidly catches up.
**Enhancements:** For residual refractive error post-SMILE, surface ablation (PRK) is the preferred enhancement method, as creating a secondary lenticule or converting to LASIK is more complex.
**Myopia Range:** SMILE is currently FDA approved for myopia up to -10.0 D and astigmatism up to -3.0 D (varies by region/device).
**Hyperopia:** SMILE for hyperopia is still in clinical trials and not yet widely available or approved.
**Suction Loss:** A critical intraoperative event, requiring immediate re-docking or conversion to PRK. Prevention through proper patient selection and docking technique is paramount.

sections.title: 15. Recent Advances & Landmark Studies
content: **Carl Zeiss Meditec VisuMax Laser:** The pioneering femtosecond laser platform for SMILE technology.
**ReLEx SMILE (Refractive Lenticule Extraction, Small Incision Lenticule Extraction):** Introduced in 2011, it revolutionized flapless refractive surgery.
**FDA Approval:** SMILE received FDA approval in the U.S. in 2016 for myopia and in 2018 for myopic astigmatism, expanding its global adoption.
**VisuMax 800:** Next-generation VisuMax laser with faster repetition rates (2 MHz) for reduced suction time and potential for even faster visual recovery.
**SMILE Pro:** Latest advancement, further optimizing the procedure with faster laser pulse, reducing treatment time to ~10 seconds.
**Topography-guided SMILE (e.g., Contoura Vision SMILE):** Emerging technology aiming to integrate topography data for personalized, even more precise lenticule creation.

sections.title: 16. Pediatric / Special Population Considerations
content: **Age Limit:** Refractive surgery is generally not recommended for individuals under 18-21 years due to unstable refraction.
**Pregnancy/Lactation:** Contraindicated due to hormonal shifts affecting corneal hydration and refraction, and potential medication effects.
**Diabetics:** Well-controlled diabetes is generally acceptable, but uncontrolled diabetes is a contraindication due to impaired healing and increased infection risk.
**Immuno-compromised:** Systemic immunosuppression (e.g., HIV, organ transplant patients on high-dose steroids) is a contraindication due to increased infection risk and poor wound healing.
**Mental Health:** Patients with unrealistic expectations or psychiatric disorders (e.g., Body Dysmorphic Disorder) are poor candidates.
**Occupational Considerations:** Specific visual requirements for pilots, military personnel may influence procedure choice.
